items.title: India's Energy Scenario & Mix
items.body:
## In one line
Where India gets its energy today — mostly coal for electricity and heavily imported oil — and why that is a problem it is trying to fix.

## The story
India's economy and population are growing, so its demand for energy keeps rising. India is now the **world's third-largest energy consumer** (after China and the USA). But because the population is so large, the **energy used per person is still well below the world average** — most Indians use far less power than the average American or European.

The worry is *where* the energy comes from. India has to **buy about 85-88% of its crude oil from abroad** (chiefly West Asia) and also imports natural gas as **LNG** (Liquefied Natural Gas — gas chilled to a liquid so it can be shipped). Spending huge sums on imported fuel, whose price can swing with global events, is the single biggest threat to India's **energy security** (a reliable, affordable supply).

For electricity, **coal is still the single largest source — it generates about 70% of India's power** even though its share of the total *installed* machinery is falling as solar and wind are added. The plan is to **phase coal down, not switch it off**: coal keeps the lights on (base-load) while clean sources are built up.

## Why it matters
Paper-II (and Mains M5-4) regularly asks the energy "big picture": import dependence, the coal-vs-clean balance, and the drivers of the transition. Getting these headline facts right anchors every other energy question.

## Picture it

| Measure | India's position |
|---|---|
| Energy consumer rank | 3rd-largest in the world |
| Energy use per person | Below the global average |
| Crude oil imported | About 85-88% |
| Largest power source | Coal (~70% of generation) |

## Terms explained
- **Energy security** — having enough energy, reliably and affordably, without being at the mercy of imports.
- **LNG** — natural gas cooled into a liquid so it can be carried by ship; India imports it.
- **Base-load** — the steady, round-the-clock electricity demand that must always be met; coal and nuclear are good at this.
- **Installed capacity vs generation** — "capacity" is how much machinery you have built; "generation" is how much electricity it actually produces. Coal's *capacity* share is falling but it still *generates* the most.

## Don't confuse
Coal leads in **generation** (electricity actually produced), but non-fossil sources now lead in **installed capacity** (machinery built). Both statements are true at the same time — a classic trap.

## Remember it
"**Import the oil, burn the coal, build the clean**" — oil mostly imported, coal still generates most, clean capacity rising fast.

## TL;DR
- India = 3rd-largest energy consumer, but low use per person.
- ~85-88% of crude oil is imported; LNG also imported — a security worry.
- Coal still generates ~70% of electricity; it is phased *down*, not banned.
- Transition drivers: net-zero 2070, energy security, cheaper renewables, cleaner air.
keyPoints: India is the world's 3rd-largest energy consumer; per-capita consumption is below the global average.
Crude oil import dependence is about 85-88 percent; India also imports LNG.
Coal is still the largest source of electricity generation (~70% of generation).
Non-fossil capacity is being added rapidly while coal is phased down, not banned.
Transition drivers: net-zero 2070, energy security, falling RE costs, air pollution.

items.title: Renewable Targets, Capacity Milestones & Solar/Wind
items.body:
## In one line
The big clean-energy targets India has set — above all the 500 GW non-fossil goal for 2030 — and the solar and wind schemes built to reach them.

## The story
At the **COP26 climate summit (Glasgow, 2021)** India announced five climate promises called **Panchamrit** ("five nectars"). The headline pledge: reach **500 GW of non-fossil installed capacity by 2030** ("non-fossil" = renewables plus nuclear plus large hydro — everything except coal, oil and gas).

India then moved faster than planned. In **June 2025 it crossed 50% of its installed electricity capacity from non-fossil sources — about five years ahead** of the target it gave the UN (its NDC). Soon after, in **September 2025, total installed capacity crossed 500 GW** (reaching ~514 GW by December 2025). An older goal of **175 GW of renewables by 2022** has been overtaken by the bigger 500 GW non-fossil goal.

**Solar** is the workhorse. The **National Solar Mission (2010)** and giant **solar parks** — Bhadla (Rajasthan) and Pavagada (Karnataka) — build large plants cheaply. **PM-KUSUM** (Pradhan Mantri Kisan Urja Suraksha evam Utthaan Mahabhiyan) is about **solarising agriculture** — it gives farmers **standalone solar pumps**, **solarises their existing grid-connected pumps**, and lets them set up small solar plants on their land and sell the surplus power. **PM Surya Ghar Muft Bijli Yojana (Feb 2024)** puts solar on rooftops — targeting **1 crore (10 million) homes**, up to **300 free units a month**, with an outlay of **Rs 75,021 crore**.

**Wind** is led by **Gujarat and Tamil Nadu**, which have the strongest coastal winds; India is now opening up **offshore wind** (turbines in the sea) with government support.

## Why it matters
"500 GW by 2030", "50% non-fossil in 2025", "net-zero 2070" and the flagship solar scheme names are among the most-asked energy facts. Numbers and years must be exact.

## Picture it

| Milestone | Figure / year |
|---|---|
| Non-fossil target | 500 GW by 2030 (Panchamrit, COP26) |
| 50% non-fossil capacity | Reached June 2025 (ahead of NDC) |
| Total installed capacity | Crossed 500 GW in Sept 2025 (~514 GW by Dec 2025) |
| PM Surya Ghar | 1 crore homes, 300 free units, Rs 75,021 cr |

## Terms explained
- **GW (gigawatt)** — a unit of power; 1 GW = 1,000 MW, roughly one large power station.
- **Non-fossil capacity** — generating machinery that does not burn coal, oil or gas (solar, wind, hydro, nuclear).
- **NDC** — Nationally Determined Contribution: the climate target a country formally promises the UN.
- **Panchamrit** — India's five COP26 pledges.
- **Solar park** — a **large contiguous zone** of land developed with **shared infrastructure** (roads, water, transmission lines to evacuate the power) where **multiple developers** each set up their own solar plants. It cuts cost and delay for every developer. Examples: Bhadla (Rajasthan), Pavagada (Karnataka), Kurnool (Andhra Pradesh).

## Don't confuse
The old **175 GW by 2022** was a *renewables-only* target; the current **500 GW by 2030** is a wider *non-fossil* target (adds nuclear and large hydro). They are different goals.

## Remember it
Panchamrit "**500-50-1-45-70**": 500 GW non-fossil, 50% energy from renewables, 1 billion-tonne CO2 cut, 45% intensity cut, net-zero by 2070.

## TL;DR
- 500 GW non-fossil by 2030, pledged at COP26 (Panchamrit).
- India hit 50% non-fossil capacity in June 2025 — 5 years early.
- Total capacity crossed 500 GW in Sept 2025.
- Solar: National Solar Mission, solar parks (Bhadla, Pavagada), PM-KUSUM (farms), PM Surya Ghar (rooftops).
- Wind leaders: Gujarat and Tamil Nadu; offshore wind beginning.

Gujarat and Tamil Nadu lead wind capacity; offshore wind is being developed.

items.title: National Green Hydrogen Mission
items.body:
## In one line
A mission to make clean "green" hydrogen fuel using renewable electricity, so India can cut oil imports and clean up heavy industry.

## The story
Hydrogen gas can be burned or used in fuel cells with **no carbon dioxide at the point of use** — only water comes out. But *making* hydrogen can be dirty. The colour tells you how it was made:
- **Grey hydrogen** — made from natural gas; releases CO2.
- **Blue hydrogen** — same, but the CO2 is captured and stored.
- **Green hydrogen** — made by **electrolysis of water** (splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen using electricity) where the **electricity comes from renewables**. This is the clean, zero-carbon kind India wants.

India approved the **National Green Hydrogen Mission in January 2023** with an initial outlay of **Rs 19,744 crore**. The aim is about **5 million tonnes (MMT) of green hydrogen a year by 2030**, backed by roughly **125 GW of extra renewable capacity** to power the electrolysis. A key component, **SIGHT** (Strategic Interventions for Green Hydrogen Transition), pays incentives for **making electrolysers** (the machines that split water) and for **producing the hydrogen**.

Why bother? Green hydrogen can replace imported fossil fuels in **fertilisers, oil refining and steel** — industries that are very hard to run on electricity alone — and India hopes to **export** it. **Andhra Pradesh**, with a long coastline and strong renewables, is building green-hydrogen hubs.

## Why it matters
Green hydrogen is a favourite current-affairs topic. Examiners test the definition (renewable electrolysis), the year and outlay, the 2030 target, and the SIGHT component.

## Picture it

| Feature | Detail |
|---|---|
| Approved | January 2023 |
| Initial outlay | Rs 19,744 crore |
| Target | ~5 MMT/year by 2030 |
| Added RE capacity | ~125 GW |
| Key scheme | SIGHT (electrolysers + production) |

## Terms explained
- **Electrolysis** — using electricity to split water into hydrogen and oxygen.
- **Electrolyser** — the machine that does electrolysis.
- **MMT** — million metric tonnes.
- **SIGHT** — the incentive programme inside the mission.

## Don't confuse
"Green" vs "grey/blue" hydrogen is only about **how it is made**, not the gas itself. Only hydrogen from **renewable** electrolysis is green.

## Remember it
"**Green = renewable split of water**" — if the electricity is clean and water is split, the hydrogen is green.

## TL;DR
- Green hydrogen = electrolysis of water using renewable power (zero carbon).
- National Green Hydrogen Mission approved Jan 2023, outlay Rs 19,744 crore.
- Target ~5 MMT/year by 2030, with ~125 GW added renewables.
- SIGHT incentivises electrolyser manufacturing and hydrogen production.
- Aims: decarbonise fertiliser/refining/steel and build an export hub.

items.title: Nuclear Energy — Three-Stage Programme, SMRs & Reforms
items.body:
## In one line
India's long-term plan to use its huge thorium reserves for nuclear power in three steps, plus the newest push for small reactors and private investment.

## The story
Nuclear power gives **firm, low-carbon electricity** that runs day and night, unlike solar and wind. India has **little uranium but a great deal of thorium**, so **Homi Bhabha** designed a **three-stage programme** to bridge that gap:
- **Stage 1 — PHWRs** (Pressurised Heavy Water Reactors) run on **natural uranium** and produce plutonium-239 as a by-product.
- **Stage 2 — Fast Breeder Reactors (FBRs)** use that plutonium with uranium-238; they *breed* (create) more fuel than they use and begin the **thorium-to-uranium-233** cycle. The **Prototype Fast Breeder Reactor (PFBR) at Kalpakkam**, run by **BHAVINI**, began **core fuel loading in March 2024** and achieved **first criticality on 6 April 2026** — the start of Stage 2.
- **Stage 3 — thorium breeders** will finally tap India's **vast thorium**, found as **monazite** sand along the beaches of Kerala, Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Andhra Pradesh.

The work is done by bodies under the **Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)**: **BARC** (research, Trombay), **IGCAR** (fast-reactor R&D, Kalpakkam), **NPCIL** (runs the commercial power plants) and **BHAVINI** (the fast breeder). **Kudankulam** (Tamil Nadu) houses Russian-built VVER reactors.

**Recent policy (2025-26).** The Union Budget 2025-26 launched a **Nuclear Energy Mission**: about **Rs 20,000 crore for Small Modular Reactor (SMR) R&D**, at least **five indigenous SMRs by 2033**, and a goal of **100 GW of nuclear by 2047** (from only ~8-9 GW today). The same budget **proposed reforms** to the **Atomic Energy Act 1962** and the **Civil Liability for Nuclear Damage Act 2010** to **open the sector to private participation** and ease liability worries (linked to the India-US 123 Agreement). Parliament then passed the **SHANTI Act, 2025** (Sustainable Harnessing and Advancement of Nuclear Energy for Transforming India, December 2025), which **replaces both Acts** and opens nuclear power to private companies; DAE released its draft rules for consultation in August–September 2026.

## Why it matters
Nuclear is tested on the three stages, the thorium-monazite link, the DAE institutions, the PFBR milestone, and the 2025-26 mission/reforms. Note the reform status carefully — the SHANTI Act, 2025 has *replaced* the 1962 and 2010 Acts.

## Picture it

| Stage | Reactor | Fuel |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | PHWR | Natural uranium → makes Pu-239 |
| 2 | FBR | Pu-239 + U-238; breeds fuel, starts Th cycle |
| 3 | Thorium breeder | Th-232 → U-233 |

## Terms explained
- **Breeder reactor** — a reactor that produces more fissile fuel than it consumes.
- **Monazite** — the sandy mineral that holds India's thorium (and rare earths).
- **SMR** — Small Modular Reactor: a compact, factory-built reactor (India's are called Bharat Small Reactors).
- **DAE** — Department of Atomic Energy, the umbrella body.

## Don't confuse
India has **limited uranium but abundant thorium** — that scarcity is the whole reason for the three-stage design. Do not swap the two.

## Remember it
Fuel ladder "**U → Pu → Th**": natural Uranium, then bred Plutonium, finally Thorium.

## TL;DR
- Three stages: PHWR (natural U) → FBR (breeds Pu, starts Th cycle) → thorium breeders.
- PFBR at Kalpakkam (BHAVINI) began core loading in 2024 and reached first criticality on 6 April 2026.
- DAE bodies: BARC (research), IGCAR (fast-reactor R&D), NPCIL (power plants), BHAVINI (FBR); Kudankulam = VVER.
- Nuclear Energy Mission (Budget 2025-26): Rs 20,000 cr SMRs, 5 SMRs by 2033, 100 GW by 2047.
- The SHANTI Act, 2025 replaced the Atomic Energy Act 1962 and the civil-liability law, opening nuclear power to private players.

items.title: Bioenergy, Energy Efficiency, EVs & Net-Zero
items.body:
## In one line
The other pillars of the transition — fuel from crops (bioenergy), using less energy (efficiency), electric vehicles, and India's global climate role.

## The story
**Bioenergy** turns plants and waste into fuel. Under the **Ethanol Blending Programme**, India mixes ethanol (alcohol made from **sugarcane, molasses, surplus grain and crop residue**) into petrol; it reached about **20% blending (E20) around 2025**, cutting oil imports and emissions. **SATAT** promotes **Compressed Bio-Gas (CBG)** made from farm and city waste, and **waste-to-energy** plants burn rubbish for power.

**Energy efficiency** means getting the same result with less energy — the cheapest "fuel" of all. The **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)** is the **statutory body coordinating energy efficiency** — "statutory" means it was created by a law, the **Energy Conservation Act 2001** — and it runs the effort. **PAT** ("Perform, Achieve and Trade") sets efficiency goals for heavy industry and lets them trade **ESCerts** (energy-saving certificates). **Star labelling** rates appliances 1-5 stars, and **UJALA** distributed cheap efficient **LED bulbs**.

**Electric vehicles (EVs)** cut oil use and city pollution. **PM E-DRIVE (2024)** replaced the earlier **FAME** schemes to subsidise EVs and build charging stations. Because solar and wind are variable, India is scaling **battery storage (BESS)** and **pumped-storage hydro** to store power for when the sun sets.

**Global role.** India pledged **net-zero by 2070** (part of Panchamrit, COP26). It co-founded the **International Solar Alliance (ISA)** with **France at CoP21 (Paris, 2015)**, **headquartered at Gurugram, India**, and leads **Mission LiFE** (a campaign for sustainable lifestyles).

## Why it matters
These supply the "other half" of energy answers — efficiency, EVs and climate diplomacy — and the ISA facts (France, 2015, Gurugram HQ) are a repeat favourite.

## Picture it

| Area | Flagship | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Bioenergy | E20, SATAT | Ethanol in petrol; bio-gas from waste |
| Efficiency | BEE, PAT, UJALA | Standards, industry trading, LED bulbs |
| Mobility | PM E-DRIVE (2024) | EV subsidies and charging |
| Climate | ISA, Mission LiFE | Solar diplomacy, green lifestyles |

## Terms explained
- **E20** — petrol with 20% ethanol blended in.
- **CBG** — Compressed Bio-Gas, a clean fuel from waste.
- **ESCerts** — tradable certificates for saving energy under PAT.
- **BESS** — Battery Energy Storage System.
- **Net-zero** — adding no more greenhouse gas to the air than you remove.

## Don't confuse
Ethanol is made from **crops and waste**, never from imported petroleum — a common trap statement.

## Remember it
"**Blend, label, drive, store, lead**": E20 blend, star labels, EV drive, battery store, ISA lead.

## TL;DR
- E20 (~20% ethanol) reached ~2025; ethanol from sugarcane/molasses/grain, not petroleum.
- SATAT promotes Compressed Bio-Gas from waste.
- BEE (EC Act 2001) runs PAT (ESCerts), star labelling and UJALA (LEDs).
- PM E-DRIVE (2024) succeeds FAME for EVs and charging.
- Net-zero by 2070; India leads ISA (with France, CoP21 2015, HQ Gurugram) and Mission LiFE.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — Energy & Pumped Storage
items.body:
## In one line
Why Andhra Pradesh is becoming a clean-energy and storage hub — strong solar/wind, a long coast for green hydrogen, and India's biggest pumped-storage potential.

## The story
Andhra Pradesh (AP) has excellent **sunshine and coastal winds** and one of India's **largest identified potentials for pumped-storage hydro projects (PSPs)** thanks to its hilly terrain and reservoirs. Its **Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024** pushes **renewables, pumped storage and green hydrogen** to attract investment and make AP a green-energy hub. AP's long **coastline** (ports such as Visakhapatnam and Kakinada) and hilly terrain are being used to attract **green-hydrogen and export-oriented investment** — hydrogen and its products (green ammonia) can be shipped abroad.

The star technology is **pumped storage — a "water battery"**. When cheap surplus power is available (midday solar), it **pumps water up to a higher reservoir**; when demand peaks (evening), it **lets the water fall back down through turbines to generate electricity**. This smooths out the ups and downs of solar and wind. AP's flagship is the **Pinnapuram Integrated Renewable Energy Storage Project in Kurnool district**, combining **solar + wind + a very large pumped-storage** unit — among the world's largest such integrated projects.

AP also keeps substantial **thermal** (coal/gas) capacity for reliable base-load and has coastal sites ideal for renewables and green hydrogen; the state has at times had **surplus power**.

## Why it matters
AP-specific energy is high-value for APPSC (and Mains M5-4). Pinnapuram, pumped storage and AP's clean-energy policy are repeat targets.

## Picture it

```
Surplus power (midday solar)  --->  PUMP water to upper reservoir
Peak demand (evening)         <---  RELEASE water through turbines -> electricity
```

## Terms explained
- **Pumped-storage hydro (PSP)** — storing energy as water lifted uphill, released later to make power.
- **Base-load** — the steady always-on demand that thermal plants reliably cover.
- **Integrated project** — one site combining several sources (solar + wind + storage).

## Don't confuse
Pumped storage does **not** create new energy — it **stores and shifts** energy from cheap times to peak times. It is a battery, not a generator of fresh power.

## Remember it
"**Pump up cheap, drop down dear**" — pump water when power is cheap, release it when power is dear (peak demand).

## TL;DR
- AP has one of India's largest pumped-storage-hydro potentials.
- AP's clean-energy policy pushes renewables, green hydrogen and storage.
- Pumped storage = pump water uphill on surplus power, generate at peak demand.
- Pinnapuram (Kurnool) integrates solar, wind and very large pumped storage.
- AP also keeps thermal capacity and has coastal sites for green hydrogen.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh — Renewable Energy Snapshot (2026)
items.body:
## In one line
The latest numbers on how much clean energy Andhra Pradesh has built by 2026 and the flagship projects behind them.

## The story
By **August 2026**, Andhra Pradesh had commissioned about **14,833 MW** of renewable energy (per NREDCAP, the state renewable-energy agency), **led by ground-mounted solar**. The mix spans solar, wind, pumped storage and rooftop solar.

The state's roadmap aims for roughly **160 GW of green energy by 2047**, with a large pipeline (~25.58 GW solar, ~5.78 GW wind, ~18.95 GW pumped storage). Flagship projects: **Pinnapuram** (Kurnool) — integrated renewables plus very large pumped storage; **Pudimadaka** (Anakapalli district, near Visakhapatnam) — an **NTPC Green hydrogen hub** — built by **NTPC Green Energy Ltd, NTPC's green-energy arm** — planned as one of India's largest green-hydrogen facilities (~1,200 tonnes/day); and the **Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park** (installed capacity about **1000 MW**) in **Panyam mandal, Kurnool district** — when commissioned (2017) it was **among the largest solar parks in the world**. These sit under the **AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024**.

**Who does what in AP's power sector**

| Entity | Full name | Function |
|---|---|---|
| APGENCO | AP Power Generation Corporation | Power generation (thermal, hydro) |
| APTRANSCO | Transmission Corporation of AP | Intra-state transmission of electricity |
| APSPCL | AP Solar Power Corporation | Development of solar parks in the state (e.g. Kurnool) |
| NREDCAP | New & Renewable Energy Development Corporation of AP | Nodal agency for new & renewable energy development |

**Don't confuse:** APGENCO **makes** the power; APTRANSCO **carries** it across the state on high-voltage lines.

## Why it matters
Current, state-specific capacity figures and project names are exactly what APPSC likes. Keep the ~14,833 MW total and the 160 GW-by-2047 target handy.

## Picture it

| Source | ~MW |
|---|---|
| Ground solar | 7,049 |
| Wind | 4,461 |
| Pumped storage | 1,680 |
| Rooftop solar | 1,015 |
| **Total RE** | **~14,833** |

## Terms explained
- **MW / GW** — megawatt / gigawatt (1 GW = 1,000 MW), units of power.
- **NREDCAP** — New & Renewable Energy Development Corporation of AP, the state nodal agency.
- **TPD** — tonnes per day (used for the Pudimadaka hydrogen hub's output).
- **Commissioned** — built and switched on (as opposed to merely planned).

## Don't confuse
AP's **~14,833 MW already commissioned (2026)** is today's reality; the **~160 GW by 2047** is a long-term *target*. Do not mix the achieved figure with the goal.

## Remember it
"**15 GW now, 160 GW by '47**" — about 15 GW commissioned today, aiming for ten times that by 2047.

## TL;DR
- AP has commissioned ~14,833 MW of renewables (NREDCAP, 2026), solar-led.
- Long-term target: ~160 GW green energy by 2047, with a big pumped-storage pipeline.
- Pinnapuram (Kurnool) integrates renewables with very large pumped storage.
- Pudimadaka (Anakapalli) NTPC Green hydrogen hub is among India's largest (~1,200 TPD).
- Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park = ~1,000 MW; under the AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024.

items.title: Conventional Energy — Coal, Oil, Gas & Hydropower in India
items.body:
## The fuels India has always relied on

**In one line:** conventional energy means fuels that are used up (coal, oil, gas) plus big hydropower; India has plenty of coal, little oil, and large untapped hydro potential in the Himalaya.

**Why it is asked:** "highest-carbon coal", "first oil field", "Strategic Petroleum Reserve sites", "coal-bed methane vs shale gas" and "tallest dam" appear again and again in APPSC, UPSC and SSC papers.

**The story**

Coal is graded by its carbon content: **anthracite** is the best, **bituminous** is the common coking and steam coal, **lignite** is soft brown coal and **peat** is the first, poorest stage. About **98% of India's coal is Gondwana coal** (about 250 million years old) in the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys; the younger **Tertiary coal** is in the North-East. **Raniganj (West Bengal)** saw India's first coal mining (1774) and **Jharia (Jharkhand)** has the best coking coal. **Neyveli (Tamil Nadu)** is the lignite centre.

Oil was first struck at **Digboi (Assam) in 1889**; Digboi also has India's oldest working refinery (1901). The offshore **Bombay High** field was found in 1974, and the **Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin** off Andhra Pradesh is the big gas province. To survive supply shocks India stores crude in underground rock caverns — the **Strategic Petroleum Reserves**.

New gas sources come from rock itself: **coal-bed methane (CBM)** is methane held inside coal seams, and **shale gas** is gas trapped in fine-grained shale that must be released by **hydraulic fracturing ("fracking")**.

### Coal, oil and gas

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Anthracite** | highest-carbon, best-quality coal (about 80–95% carbon); found mainly in Jammu & Kashmir |
| **Lignite** | low-grade brown coal — mined at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu |
| **Peat** | first stage of coal formation; lowest carbon, high moisture |
| **Gondwana coal** | about 98% of India's coal reserves (Damodar, Mahanadi, Godavari valleys) |
| **Tertiary coal** | younger coal of the North-East (Assam, Meghalaya) |
| **Jharia (Jharkhand)** | largest reserve of coking coal used in steel making |
| **Raniganj (West Bengal)** | first coal mining in India (1774); first commercial coal-bed methane |
| **Digboi (Assam)** | first oil discovered in India (1889); oldest working refinery (1901) |
| **Bombay High** | largest offshore oil field, discovered in 1974 |
| **Krishna-Godavari (KG) basin** | major offshore gas province off Andhra Pradesh (KG-D6) |
| **Strategic Petroleum Reserves (ISPRL)** | underground caverns at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur — about 5.33 million tonnes |
| **Coal-bed methane (CBM)** | methane gas held inside coal seams |
| **Shale gas** | gas trapped in shale rock, released by hydraulic fracturing (fracking) |

### Hydropower

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Sidrapong, Darjeeling (1897)** | India's first hydroelectric plant |
| **Shivanasamudra (Karnataka, 1902)** | first major hydroelectric station in Asia, on the Kaveri |
| **Tehri Dam** | India's tallest dam, on the Bhagirathi in Uttarakhand |
| **Bhakra Nangal** | multipurpose project on the Sutlej (Himachal Pradesh–Punjab) |
| **Small hydro** | plants up to 25 MW — counted under MNRE as renewable |
| **Large hydro (above 25 MW)** | declared renewable energy in March 2019 |
| **Brahmaputra basin** | holds nearly half of India's untapped hydro potential |

## Don't confuse
- **Anthracite = best coal; lignite = brown coal (Neyveli); peat = poorest, first stage.**
- **CBM** comes from **coal seams**; **shale gas** comes from **shale** and needs **fracking**.
- **Digboi (1889) = first oil; Bombay High (1974) = biggest offshore field; KG basin = east-coast gas.**
- **Small hydro = up to 25 MW.** Large hydro has also counted as renewable since 2019.

**Remember it:** "A-B-L-P" — Anthracite, Bituminous, Lignite, Peat: from best to poorest coal.

**TL;DR**
- Gondwana coal is about 98% of reserves; Jharia = coking coal; Neyveli = lignite; Raniganj = first mining (1774).
- Oil: Digboi 1889, Bombay High 1974; gas: KG basin; crude stored at Visakhapatnam, Mangaluru and Padur.
- Hydro: Sidrapong 1897 first plant; Tehri is the tallest dam; small hydro is up to 25 MW.
keyPoints: Anthracite — highest-carbon, best-quality coal (about 80–95% carbon); found mainly in Jammu & Kashmir.
Lignite — low-grade brown coal — mined at Neyveli, Tamil Nadu.
Tehri Dam — India's tallest dam, on the Bhagirathi in Uttarakhand.
Small hydro — plants up to 25 MW — counted under MNRE as renewable.

items.title: Non-Conventional Energy Technologies — How They Work
items.body:
## The clean technologies, one by one

**In one line:** non-conventional (renewable) energy uses flows that never run out — sunlight, wind, tides, the Earth's heat, ocean warmth, plants and waste — and each has one working principle examiners ask about.

**Why it is asked:** "photovoltaic vs solar thermal", "a fuel cell gives which by-product?", "geothermal site in Ladakh", "tidal potential in the Gulf of Khambhat" and "what is OTEC?" are classic statement and match items.

**The story**

A **solar (photovoltaic, PV) cell**, usually made of **silicon**, turns sunlight straight into electricity by the photovoltaic effect. **Solar thermal** systems instead use the Sun's heat — to warm water or, with mirrors, to raise steam (concentrated solar power). A **wind turbine** turns the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity. **Tidal** power uses the rise and fall of the sea; **wave** power uses surface waves. **Geothermal** energy taps heat from inside the Earth, as at **Puga Valley in Ladakh**. **OTEC (Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion)** runs a heat engine on the temperature difference — about 20 °C or more — between warm surface water and cold deep water. A **fuel cell** combines hydrogen and oxygen to make electricity directly, giving only **water and heat**.

### Technologies and principles

| Technology | How it works / fact |
|---|---|
| **Solar photovoltaic (PV) cell** | converts sunlight directly into electricity; usually made of silicon |
| **Solar thermal / concentrated solar power** | uses the Sun's heat — water heaters, or mirrors raising steam for turbines |
| **Perovskite solar cell** | new low-cost thin-film cell material under development |
| **Bifacial solar module** | panel that captures light on both faces |
| **Floating solar** | panels on reservoirs — e.g. Omkareshwar (Narmada, Madhya Pradesh) and Ramagundam (Telangana) |
| **Wind turbine** | converts the kinetic energy of moving air into electricity |
| **Tidal energy** | uses the rise and fall of tides — best sites Gulf of Khambhat and Gulf of Kutch (Gujarat), Sundarbans |
| **Geothermal energy** | heat from inside the Earth — Puga Valley (Ladakh), Manikaran (Himachal), Tattapani (Chhattisgarh) |
| **OTEC (Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion)** | uses the temperature difference (20 °C or more) between warm surface and cold deep sea water |
| **Low-Temperature Thermal Desalination (LTTD)** | NIOT plant at Kavaratti, Lakshadweep, uses the same ocean temperature gap to make drinking water |
| **Fuel cell** | combines hydrogen and oxygen to give electricity; by-products only water and heat |
| **Biogas** | mainly methane, made by anaerobic digestion of dung and waste |
| **Biomass gasifier** | turns wood or crop waste into a combustible producer gas |
| **Second-generation (2G) ethanol** | made from crop residue such as rice straw — IOCL plant at Panipat (2022) |

### Renewable energy institutes (under MNRE)

| Institute | Location |
|---|---|
| **National Institute of Solar Energy (NISE)** | Gurugram, Haryana |
| **National Institute of Wind Energy (NIWE)** | Chennai, Tamil Nadu |
| **Sardar Swaran Singh National Institute of Bio-Energy** | Kapurthala, Punjab |

## Don't confuse
- **Photovoltaic = light → electricity directly; solar thermal = the Sun's heat.**
- **Tidal** uses tides (Gulf of Khambhat); **OTEC** uses the **temperature difference** between surface and deep water; **wave** energy uses surface waves.
- A **fuel cell** is not a battery that needs charging — it runs as long as hydrogen is fed, and gives only water.
- **Biogas** is mostly **methane**; **CBG** is purified, compressed biogas.

**Remember it:** "PV sees light, thermal feels heat, OTEC feels the gap."

**TL;DR**
- Solar PV (silicon) turns light into power; solar thermal uses heat.
- Tidal: Gulf of Khambhat, Kutch, Sundarbans; geothermal: Puga (Ladakh), Manikaran, Tattapani.
- OTEC needs about 20 °C between surface and deep water; fuel cell gives only water and heat.
- NISE Gurugram, NIWE Chennai, Bio-Energy institute Kapurthala.
keyPoints: Solar photovoltaic (PV) cell — converts sunlight directly into electricity; usually made of silicon.
Solar thermal / concentrated solar power — uses the Sun's heat — water heaters, or mirrors raising steam for turbines.

items.title: India's Installed Clean-Energy Capacity — the Numbers (30 September 2026)
items.body:
## How much clean power India has built

**In one line:** by 30 September 2026 India had about **308 GW of non-fossil capacity** — about 171 GW solar, 59 GW wind, 52 GW large hydro, about 16 GW bio-power and small hydro, and about 8.8 GW nuclear (MNRE).

**Why it is asked:** "India's rank in solar capacity", "largest renewable source", "largest solar park" and "which ministry was the world's first for renewables" are standard current-affairs-cum-static items.

**The story**

**Solar** has become India's biggest clean source, at about **171 GW** — most of it ground-mounted parks, with about **33 GW of rooftop solar**. **Wind** comes next at about **59 GW**. **Large hydro** is about **52 GW** (this figure includes about 7.4 GW of pumped storage). Altogether, renewables including large hydro are about **299 GW**, and adding nuclear gives about **308 GW non-fossil**. India is the **third-largest country in the world for renewable and solar capacity** (after China and the USA) and **fourth for wind**. India was also the first country with a ministry for non-conventional energy: the **Department of Non-Conventional Energy Sources (1982)** became a ministry in 1992 and was renamed the **Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE) in 2006**.

### Capacity and rankings (MNRE, 30 September 2026)

| Measure | Figure |
|---|---|
| **Solar capacity** | about 171 GW — the largest renewable source |
| **Wind capacity** | about 59 GW — second-largest renewable source |
| **Large hydro capacity** | about 52 GW, including about 7.4 GW pumped storage |
| **Rooftop solar** | about 33 GW grid-connected |
| **Total non-fossil capacity** | about 308 GW (renewables about 299 GW plus nuclear about 8.8 GW) |
| **Nuclear capacity** | about 8.8 GW — the smallest non-fossil share |
| **India's world rank** | 3rd in renewable and in solar capacity; 4th in wind |
| **Bhadla Solar Park (Jodhpur, Rajasthan)** | India's largest commissioned solar park (about 2,245 MW) |
| **Pavagada Solar Park (Karnataka)** | India's second-largest solar park |
| **Khavda (Rann of Kutch, Gujarat)** | 30 GW hybrid renewable energy park — set to be the world's largest |
| **Ministry of New and Renewable Energy** | began as a Department in 1982 — the world's first such ministry; renamed MNRE in 2006 |

## Don't confuse
- **Solar (about 171 GW) > wind (about 59 GW) > large hydro (about 52 GW) > bio-power > nuclear (about 8.8 GW).**
- **Bhadla (Rajasthan)** is the largest commissioned solar park; **Khavda (Gujarat)** is the giant 30 GW hybrid park being built; **Pavagada** is in Karnataka; **Kurnool** and **NP Kunta** are in Andhra Pradesh.
- Capacity figures change every month — learn the order of size and the round numbers, not the decimals.

**Remember it:** "Sun 171, wind 59, water 52, atom 9 — about 308 non-fossil."

**TL;DR**
- Non-fossil about 308 GW (Sept 2026): solar 171, wind 59, large hydro 52, nuclear 8.8.
- India ranks 3rd in renewable and solar capacity, 4th in wind.
- Bhadla largest solar park; Khavda 30 GW hybrid park; MNRE began as a department in 1982.
keyPoints: Solar capacity — about 171 GW — the largest renewable source.
Wind capacity — about 59 GW — second-largest renewable source.

items.title: Nuclear Reactors, Power Plants & the Atomic Energy Bodies
items.body:
## Where India splits the atom

**In one line:** India's nuclear story runs from Asia's first research reactor, Apsara (1956), and the first power station at Tarapur (1969) to the 500 MWe PFBR going critical in 2026 — with each plant tied to one state and often to one foreign partner.

**Why it is asked:** "first nuclear power station", "Kudankulam built with which country", "only U-233 reactor", "Kovvada is in which district" and "which body regulates nuclear safety" are favourite match items.

**The story**

The **Atomic Energy Commission (1948)** and the **Department of Atomic Energy (DAE, 1954)** set up the programme under **Homi Bhabha**. **Apsara (1956)** at Trombay was **Asia's first research reactor**. India's first power station, **Tarapur (Maharashtra, 1969)**, used American boiling-water reactors. India then standardised on **PHWRs** (pressurised heavy water reactors), which use **heavy water** as moderator and coolant, and in **2020–23 Kakrapar-3** became the **first indigenous 700 MWe PHWR**. Safety is overseen by the **Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB, 1983)**. After the **India–US 123 Agreement (2008)** and the Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver (2008), India could buy foreign reactors and fuel. Uranium is mined by the **Uranium Corporation of India (UCIL)** — first at **Jaduguda (Jharkhand)** — and **Tummalapalle (Kadapa, Andhra Pradesh)** holds one of the world's largest uranium deposits.

### Reactors and power plants

| Reactor / plant | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Apsara (Trombay, 1956)** | Asia's first research reactor |
| **Tarapur (Maharashtra, 1969)** | India's first nuclear power station — boiling-water reactors from the USA |
| **Rawatbhata (RAPS), Rajasthan** | first PHWR station, built with Canadian (CANDU) help |
| **Kakrapar-3 (Gujarat)** | first indigenous 700 MWe PHWR |
| **Kudankulam (Tamil Nadu)** | India's largest nuclear plant — Russian VVER-1000 reactors |
| **KAMINI (Kalpakkam, 1996)** | the world's only reactor running on uranium-233 fuel |
| **PFBR (Kalpakkam)** | 500 MWe sodium-cooled fast breeder using MOX fuel — first criticality 6 April 2026 |
| **Kaiga** | PHWR station in Karnataka |
| **Narora** | PHWR station in Uttar Pradesh |
| **Gorakhpur (Haryana)** | upcoming 700 MWe PHWR station (GHAVP) |
| **Jaitapur (Maharashtra)** | planned with France (EPR reactors) — would be the largest nuclear site |
| **Kovvada (Srikakulam, Andhra Pradesh)** | planned with the USA (Westinghouse AP1000 reactors) |

### Atomic energy bodies and agreements

| Body / item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Atomic Energy Commission** | set up in 1948, chaired first by Homi Bhabha |
| **Department of Atomic Energy (DAE)** | created in 1954, directly under the Prime Minister |
| **BARC** | began as AEET (1954); renamed Bhabha Atomic Research Centre in 1967 |
| **Atomic Energy Regulatory Board (AERB)** | nuclear safety regulator, set up in 1983 |
| **Uranium Corporation of India (UCIL)** | mines uranium; India's first uranium mine at Jaduguda, Jharkhand |
| **Tummalapalle (Kadapa, Andhra Pradesh)** | one of the world's largest uranium deposits |
| **IREL (Indian Rare Earths Ltd)** | processes monazite beach sands for thorium and rare earths |
| **Heavy water (D2O)** | moderator and coolant in PHWRs — made by the Heavy Water Board |
| **India–US 123 Agreement (2008)** | civil nuclear cooperation deal; came with the NSG waiver of 2008 |
| **ITER (Cadarache, France)** | international nuclear-fusion experiment; India a member since 2005 |
| **Bharat Small Reactors** | 220 MWe PHWRs offered for captive industrial power under the Nuclear Energy Mission |

## Don't confuse
- **Apsara (1956) = first research reactor; Tarapur (1969) = first power station.**
- **Kudankulam = Russia; Jaitapur = France; Kovvada (AP) = USA.**
- **KAMINI** runs on **U-233**; **PFBR** is a **sodium-cooled fast breeder** (Stage 2).
- **Fission** (splitting heavy atoms) runs today's reactors; **fusion** (joining light atoms, as in the Sun) is what ITER is testing.

**Remember it:** "Russia-Kudankulam, France-Jaitapur, America-Kovvada."

**TL;DR**
- AEC 1948, DAE 1954, AERB 1983; BARC named in 1967.
- Apsara 1956, Tarapur 1969, Kakrapar-3 first 700 MWe indigenous PHWR, PFBR critical 6 April 2026.
- Uranium: Jaduguda (first mine), Tummalapalle (AP, huge deposit); thorium from monazite (IREL).
keyPoints: Apsara (Trombay, 1956) — Asia's first research reactor.
Tarapur (Maharashtra, 1969) — India's first nuclear power station — boiling-water reactors from the USA.
Atomic Energy Commission — set up in 1948, chaired first by Homi Bhabha.
Department of Atomic Energy (DAE) — created in 1954, directly under the Prime Minister.

items.title: Energy Laws, Institutions & Schemes — the Who-Does-What List
items.body:
## The rulebook and the agencies

**In one line:** a handful of laws (Energy Conservation Act 2001, Electricity Act 2003, SHANTI Act 2025) and agencies (BEE, SECI, IREDA, CEA, CERC, EESL) run India's energy sector, and each scheme has one target group.

**Why it is asked:** "BEE was set up under which Act", "SECI is the implementing agency for", "the last village electrified", "UDAY was for", "Global Biofuels Alliance launched at" are typical statement and match items.

**The story**

The **Energy Conservation Act 2001** created the **Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE, 2002)**; its **2022 amendment** allowed a national **carbon market**, now run as the **Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023)**. The **Electricity Act 2003** set up the regulator system (CERC at the centre, SERCs in states) and freed power generation from licensing. Electrification came in two steps: **DDUGJY (2014)** wired every village — the last, **Leisang in Manipur, on 28 April 2018** — and **Saubhagya (2017)** connected the remaining households. **UDAY (2015)** and **RDSS (2021, smart meters)** tried to fix loss-making distribution companies (discoms). For biofuels, the **National Policy on Biofuels 2018** (amended 2022) brought the E20 target forward to 2025-26, and India launched the **Global Biofuels Alliance at the G20 New Delhi summit (2023)**.

### Laws and agencies

| Law / agency | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022** | enabled a carbon market — the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023) |
| **Electricity Act 2003** | set up CERC/SERCs, open access and licence-free generation |
| **CERC** | Central Electricity Regulatory Commission — fixes inter-state tariffs |
| **Central Electricity Authority (CEA)** | statutory technical adviser and planner for the power sector |
| **SECI (2011)** | Solar Energy Corporation of India — implementing agency for the National Solar Mission |
| **IREDA (1987)** | Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency — lends to clean-energy projects |
| **EESL** | Energy Efficiency Services Ltd — runs UJALA and street-lighting LEDs |
| **NTPC (1975)** | India's largest power producer; NTPC Green Energy is its renewables arm |
| **NAPCC (2008)** | eight missions, including the National Solar Mission and the Mission for Enhanced Energy Efficiency (PAT) |

### Schemes and programmes

| Scheme | What it does |
|---|---|
| **DDUGJY (2014)** | village electrification — last village Leisang (Manipur), 28 April 2018 |
| **Saubhagya (2017)** | electricity connection for every household |
| **UDAY (2015)** | financial turnaround of state discoms |
| **RDSS (2021)** | Revamped Distribution Sector Scheme — smart prepaid meters, loss reduction |
| **Green Energy Corridor** | transmission lines to carry renewable power to the grid |
| **National Policy on Biofuels 2018 (amended 2022)** | advanced the E20 target from 2030 to 2025-26 |
| **PM JI-VAN Yojana (2019)** | funds second-generation (2G) ethanol plants |
| **GOBAR-Dhan (2018)** | turns cattle dung and farm waste into biogas and CBG |
| **PLI for high-efficiency solar PV modules (2021)** | production-linked incentive to make solar modules in India |
| **ALMM** | Approved List of Models and Manufacturers — only listed Indian-made modules for government-backed projects |
| **National Offshore Wind Energy Policy (2015)** | opened sea-based wind; best sites off Gujarat and Tamil Nadu |
| **National Wind-Solar Hybrid Policy (2018)** | wind and solar plants sharing one site and grid link |
| **FAME I (2015) and FAME II (2019)** | earlier EV subsidy schemes, succeeded by PM E-DRIVE (2024) |

### Global energy bodies

| Body | Fact |
|---|---|
| **International Solar Alliance (ISA)** | treaty-based body since December 2017 — first intergovernmental organisation headquartered in India |
| **One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG)** | India's proposal (2018) for a global solar grid, pursued with ISA |
| **Global Biofuels Alliance** | launched by India at the G20 New Delhi summit, September 2023 |
| **IRENA** | International Renewable Energy Agency (2009), HQ Abu Dhabi |
| **International Energy Agency (IEA)** | Paris-based OECD body; India is an association country (since 2017), not a full member |
| **OPEC** | oil exporters' cartel (1960), HQ Vienna; India is not a member |
| **Mission Innovation** | launched at COP21 Paris (2015) to double clean-energy R&D |

## Don't confuse
- **BEE** (efficiency rules) was created by the **Energy Conservation Act 2001**; **EESL** is the company that actually distributes LEDs under **UJALA**.
- **SECI** carries out solar auctions; **IREDA** lends money; **CEA** plans; **CERC** sets tariffs.
- **DDUGJY = villages (done April 2018, Leisang); Saubhagya = households.**
- **ISA HQ = Gurugram; IRENA HQ = Abu Dhabi; IEA HQ = Paris; OPEC HQ = Vienna.**

**Remember it:** "BEE sets the rules, EESL sells the bulbs, SECI holds the auctions, IREDA pays."

**TL;DR**
- EC Act 2001 → BEE; 2022 amendment → carbon market (CCTS 2023); Electricity Act 2003 → CERC/SERCs.
- DDUGJY 2014 (last village Leisang, 2018), Saubhagya 2017, UDAY 2015, RDSS 2021.
- Biofuels Policy 2018 (E20 by 2025-26), PM JI-VAN (2G ethanol), GOBAR-Dhan, Global Biofuels Alliance (G20, 2023).
- ISA (treaty body 2017, Gurugram), IRENA (Abu Dhabi), OSOWOG.
keyPoints: Energy Conservation (Amendment) Act 2022 — enabled a carbon market — the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (2023).
Electricity Act 2003 — set up CERC/SERCs, open access and licence-free generation.
DDUGJY (2014) — village electrification — last village Leisang (Manipur), 28 April 2018.
Saubhagya (2017) — electricity connection for every household.
International Solar Alliance (ISA) — treaty-based body since December 2017 — first intergovernmental organisation headquartered in India.
One Sun One World One Grid (OSOWOG) — India's proposal (2018) for a global solar grid, pursued with ISA.

items.title: Andhra Pradesh Power Map — Plants, Fuels & Projects
items.body:
## Every power source in Andhra Pradesh, by place

**In one line:** Andhra Pradesh mixes coal plants on the coast and in Rayalaseema, old hydro stations on the Krishna and the Sileru, huge solar parks in Rayalaseema, gas and an oil reserve on the coast, a planned nuclear plant at Kovvada and a uranium deposit at Tummalapalle.

**Why it is asked:** APPSC likes "match the AP power station with its district/river", "where is the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in AP" and "which AP solar park is in Panyam / NP Kunta".

**The story**

On the coast, NTPC's **Simhadri** station near **Visakhapatnam** and APGENCO's **Dr Narla Tata Rao station (Vijayawada)** and **Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah station (Krishnapatnam, Nellore)** burn coal, while the **Rayalaseema Thermal Power Station** is at **Muddanur (Kadapa)**. Hydro power comes from **Srisailam (Krishna)**, the **Upper and Lower Sileru** stations, the joint AP–Odisha **Machkund** project and, when complete, **Polavaram** on the Godavari. Rayalaseema's dry, sunny land hosts the **Kurnool (Panyam)** and **NP Kunta (Ananthapuram-I)** ultra mega solar parks and the **Pinnapuram** integrated project. **Visakhapatnam** has India's **first Strategic Petroleum Reserve** and an HPCL refinery, and the **KG basin** supplies offshore gas.

### Andhra Pradesh power and fuel sites

| Site | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Simhadri Super Thermal Power Station** | NTPC coal plant near Visakhapatnam (about 2,000 MW) |
| **Dr Narla Tata Rao Thermal Power Station** | APGENCO coal plant at Vijayawada (Ibrahimpatnam) |
| **Sri Damodaram Sanjeevaiah Thermal Power Station** | APGENCO coal plant at Krishnapatnam, Nellore district |
| **Rayalaseema Thermal Power Station** | APGENCO coal plant at Muddanur, Kadapa district |
| **Srisailam hydro station** | on the Krishna — right-bank station run by APGENCO |
| **Upper and Lower Sileru** | hydro stations on the Sileru, a Godavari tributary |
| **Machkund** | joint Andhra Pradesh–Odisha hydro project |
| **Polavaram** | multipurpose Godavari project with a 960 MW hydro station |
| **NP Kunta (Ananthapuram-I) Ultra Mega Solar Park** | Nambulapulakunta mandal, Rayalaseema — first phase commissioned 2016 |
| **Visakhapatnam Strategic Petroleum Reserve** | India's first SPR cavern (about 1.33 million tonnes) |
| **HPCL Visakh refinery** | oil refinery at Visakhapatnam |
| **KG-D6** | Reliance deep-water gas block in the Krishna-Godavari basin |
| **Pinnapuram project developer** | Greenko — about 1,680 MW of pumped storage with solar and wind |

## Don't confuse
- **Simhadri (NTPC) = Visakhapatnam; Narla Tata Rao = Vijayawada; Krishnapatnam = Nellore; Muddanur = Kadapa.**
- **Kurnool UMSP = Panyam mandal; NP Kunta UMSP = Nambulapulakunta mandal; Pinnapuram = pumped storage in Kurnool district.**
- **Kovvada (Srikakulam)** is a planned nuclear plant; **Tummalapalle (Kadapa)** is a uranium deposit — not a power plant.

**Remember it:** "Coal on the coast, water in the Krishna and Sileru, sun in Rayalaseema, oil under Vizag."

**TL;DR**
- Thermal: Simhadri (Vizag), Narla Tata Rao (Vijayawada), Krishnapatnam (Nellore), Muddanur (Kadapa).
- Hydro: Srisailam, Sileru, Machkund (with Odisha), Polavaram (960 MW).
- Solar: Kurnool (Panyam), NP Kunta; storage: Pinnapuram (Greenko); oil: Visakhapatnam SPR; gas: KG basin.
keyPoints: Simhadri Super Thermal Power Station — NTPC coal plant near Visakhapatnam (about 2,000 MW).
Srisailam hydro station — on the Krishna — right-bank station run by APGENCO.

items.title: For Mains — Energy Resources & Policy
items.body:
## In one line
How to turn the energy facts into a strong Mains answer for Paper-V (M5-4: energy needs, clean energy, conventional/non-conventional and nuclear policy).

## The dimensions Mains asks

| Dimension | What to write |
|---|---|
| Status / context | 3rd-largest consumer; ~85-88% crude imported; coal still ~70% of generation |
| Targets & achievements | Panchamrit: 500 GW non-fossil by 2030, net-zero 2070; 50% non-fossil reached June 2025 (early) |
| Clean-energy push | Solar (PM Surya Ghar, PM-KUSUM, parks), Green Hydrogen Mission, E20/SATAT, PM E-DRIVE, storage |
| Nuclear policy | Three-stage programme, PFBR critical April 2026, Nuclear Energy Mission (SMRs, 100 GW by 2047), SHANTI Act 2025 private entry |
| Challenges | Grid integration of variable RE, storage gap, discom financial stress, land & finance, just transition from coal |
| Way forward | Scale storage (battery + pumped hydro), grid reform, green-hydrogen for hard-to-abate sectors, just transition |

## Data points to quote
- 50% non-fossil installed capacity reached **June 2025**; total capacity crossed **500 GW (Sept 2025, ~514 GW by Dec 2025)**.
- National Green Hydrogen Mission (2023, **Rs 19,744 cr**, ~5 MMT by 2030).
- Nuclear Energy Mission (Budget 2025-26, **Rs 20,000 cr** SMRs, **100 GW by 2047**).
- ISA (India-France, CoP21 2015, HQ Gurugram); Mission LiFE.

## AP angle
AP is a natural **balancing and green-fuel hub**: one of India's largest pumped-storage potentials (**Pinnapuram, Kurnool**), the **Pudimadaka** NTPC green-hydrogen hub (~1,200 TPD), **Kurnool Ultra Mega Solar Park**, and the **AP Integrated Clean Energy Policy 2024** targeting ~160 GW green energy by 2047.

## Use in answers
- **Example:** cite India reaching 50% non-fossil capacity five years early as proof of a credible transition.
- **Quote:** frame energy as the "trilemma" of security, affordability and sustainability.
- **Diagram idea:** a simple triangle of Energy Security - Affordability - Sustainability, or a flow of surplus solar -> pumped storage -> peak supply.

## TL;DR
- Structure: status -> targets -> missions -> challenges -> way forward, with an AP paragraph.
- Lead with the 50%-by-2025 achievement and the storage/just-transition challenge.
- Always weave in AP's pumped storage and green hydrogen for the state angle.
